clue.text: Rasher gnarl?

parts.note: said out loud, these two words sound like the word rational, a word for reasoned thought; so they are a reasoning word voiced

explanation.surface: A grumpy remark about a strip of bacon that has gone tough and knobbly.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'rasher gnarl' quickly in a non-rhotic British accent and you hear 'rational': a thinking word, spoken aloud. The question mark flags the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Voicing your reasoning as you go is the idiom for musing audibly, and 'rational' voiced is what the clue literally shows.

clue.text: Awful Roosevelt gaffe: he's half admitted battle's about to commence

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so this letter goes inside the others
an awful gaffe is a mangled one, so these letters are jumbled
half of the two-letter word he, the first letter only, is taken

explanation.surface: A US president makes a terrible blunder, half-confessing that war is imminent.
explanation.walkthrough: The H from half of 'he' goes into the rearranged ROOSEVELT GAFFE.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom says a fight is now to be waged without restraint, taken from boxers shedding their padding.

clue.text: Easily heading off express, but not by direct route

definitions.text: express, but not by direct route

indicators.note: the heading, the first letter, is cut off

parts.note: to do something simply is to do it easily

explanation.surface: Simply driving off on a motorway, but taking a roundabout way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Express' looks like a fast road, but it is a verb in the definition: to say indirectly.
explanation.definitionFit: To suggest something without stating it is to convey it indirectly, which is what the phrase describes.

clue.text: How many million people could this sports revolutionary get into SW Ireland?

definitions.text: How many million people could this sports revolutionary get into SW Ireland?

parts.words: How many million people could this sports revolutionary get into SW Ireland
parts.note: the southwestern Irish county is Kerry; that is also the name of the Australian tycoon who shook up cricket

explanation.surface: Asks how many millions of people some sporting radical could squeeze into an Irish county.
explanation.walkthrough: Kerry Packer, the Australian media owner, launched breakaway World Series Cricket in 1977. Kerry is a county in south-west Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Australian mogul transformed cricket with his rebel World Series, so he fits as a sports revolutionary.

clue.text: Chocolatier's daughter got comfy

parts.note: Nestlé is the Swiss confectionery maker

explanation.surface: A confectioner's girl made herself cosy.
explanation.definitionFit: To settle snugly against something is to get cosy and comfortable.

clue.text: Single shot at goal's saved, a pain for those attending

indicators.note: has saved means holds, so the other letters keep this one safe inside them
something shot is ruined or wrecked, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral, is single

explanation.surface: A lone attempt at goal is stopped, annoying the spectators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Those attending' are listeners, so the pain is in the ear; 'shot' and 'saved' borrow football language.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the medical term for earache, a pain for anyone listening hard.

clue.text: Kick in final third of game (see 25)

indicators.note: only the last of the game's three parts is kept, the other two dropped

parts.note: the game of noughts and crosses is called tic-tac-toe

explanation.surface: A kick in the last period of a match, with a pointer to another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Tic-tac-toe is the American name for noughts and crosses; 25-down uses its first part.
explanation.definitionFit: To strike a ball with the tip of the foot is a toe-poke, a type of kick.

clue.text: Better garden party?

definitions.meaning: to better someone is to surpass them
a do held outside, an ..., as a whimsical reading

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer as OUT (outdoors) and DO (a party).
explanation.definitionFit: To surpass a rival is to do better than them, and a party in the open is an outdoor do.

clue.text: National spot animal park employee patrols you should visit more often

indicators.note: the spot patrols around national, going round it

parts.note: a spot is a dot
a beast is an animal
a ranger looks after a park

explanation.surface: A national park warden watches over a particular creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patrols' reads as the ranger's job, but it is the container signal: the spot goes round National.
explanation.definitionFit: The farewell phrase asks a friend to come round again soon, urging more frequent calls.

clue.text: New York Times quote, out of Time

indicators.note: music played out of time has lost its order and rhythm, so these letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: to quote words is to repeat them

explanation.surface: A New York newspaper quotation that doesn't appear in Time magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New York Times' reads as the paper, but the definition stops at 'New York'. TIMES plus REPEAT, rearranged, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: New York's nickname is this phrase, also the name of its famous skyscraper building.

clue.text: Quite a few late-night shows

indicators.note: the word shows means the answer is on display within the letters of late-night

explanation.surface: There are plenty of television programmes broadcast late at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shows' looks like the TV programmes but it is the signal that the letters are displayed inside 'late-night'.
explanation.definitionFit: A number of that size counts as a fair handful, which is what quite a few loosely means.

clue.text: Resting place of people past

parts.note: the lay are ordinary people, as opposed to the clergy
by can mean past, as in walking by

explanation.surface: Sounds like a cemetery: the resting place of people from times gone by.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a grave. A LAY-BY is a British roadside pull-in where drivers stop and rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside parking bay is where a motorist pulls over to take a break.

clue.text: Redesigning BBC logo, I'm giving malicious instructions

indicators.note: redesigning something reworks its parts, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A designer revamping the BBC's emblem admits to slipping in harmful orders.
explanation.definitionFit: This is hidden program code set to do damage when a condition is met, a kind of malware.

clue.text: Plant fish inside, did someone say?

indicators.note: did someone say asks how the words sound when spoken

parts.note: a carp is a fish and the interior is the inside, so the phrase is carp interior

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they heard about planting a fish indoors.
explanation.walkthrough: Carpenteria is a Californian evergreen shrub, the tree anemone.
explanation.definitionFit: The genus is a flowering evergreen shrub from California, so it is a kind of garden shrub.

clue.text: Blathering Blair overheard by aides, brushing off that fateful day?

definitions.text: Blathering Blair overheard by aides, brushing off that fateful day?

indicators.note: blathering is talking confusedly, so these letters are jumbled
brushing something off removes it, so these letters are taken out of the word aides

parts.note: the Ides of March, the day Caesar was killed, is the classic fateful day

explanation.surface: Tony Blair is heard babbling by his staff, who shrug off talk of a day of reckoning.
explanation.walkthrough: AIDES less IDES leaves A; BLAIR, OVERHEARD and A are rearranged. 'by' just joins. The whole clue also describes the answer: a politician caught in endless chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the jokey idiom for an unstoppable flow of words, exactly what blathering is.

clue.text: This gypsy gentleman's conveying irony in broadcast

indicators.note: in broadcast means as heard on air, spoken

parts.note: something conveying irony is wry

explanation.surface: A Romany gentleman is being ironic on air.
explanation.walkthrough: A rye is a Romany word for a gentleman, as in George Borrow's 'The Romany Rye'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Romany speech the word means a gentleman, made familiar by Borrow's novel.

clue.text: Textbook Gordon Bennett!

parts.note: the text-message equivalent of the old exclamation of surprise Gordon Bennett, as written in phone shorthand

explanation.surface: A perfect example of someone shouting a cry of astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gordon Bennett!' is an old British exclamation of surprise; 'textbook' read as text-book means in text-speak.
explanation.definitionFit: The texting shorthand for an exclamation of disbelief does the same job as that old cry.

clue.text: British people, previously sickly in appearance, saying Mass?

indicators.note: in says the run of synonyms sits inside the word for appearance

parts.note: sight can mean appearance, as in a sight for sore eyes

indicators.note: previously says the sickly word comes before the others

parts.note: peaky is British slang for looking pale and unwell
our, as in our country, stands for British from a British setter's viewpoint
we are people speaking of themselves

explanation.surface: Britons who once looked poorly are now saying a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mass' looks like the church service, but it is weight. The answer is the old coin-operated machine, once common in British stations and piers, that announced your weight aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: The machine's voice tells the user their body mass, so it is something saying mass.

clue.text: In big trouble earls about to have a row? Probably not

definitions.text: about to have a row? Probably not

indicators.note: In says the rearranged earls sit within big

parts.note: OS is the abbreviation for outsize, big

indicators.note: troubled earls are stirred up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Some noblemen in serious difficulty are on the verge of arguing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' rhymes with 'cow' on the surface, but here it means to pull oars. OS is a clothing size.
explanation.definitionFit: A boat without oars can't be rowed, so someone in it is unlikely to row.

clue.text: East German breaks into rather indecent repartee

indicators.note: breaks into means goes inside

parts.note: ripe language is somewhat crude
Ost is German for east

explanation.surface: An East German interrupts a fairly smutty exchange of banter.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick retort is the core of repartee, witty back-and-forth answers.

clue.text: Does it pick up those on a criminal charge?

definitions.text: Does it pick up those on a criminal charge?

parts.words: Does it pick up those on a criminal charge
parts.note: a charge is also a rush at speed, so those on a criminal charge are speeding drivers, which a roadside detector picks up

explanation.surface: Asks whether something catches people who have been accused of a crime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' reads as an accusation, but here it means a dash: speeders, caught by a speed-detecting device.
explanation.definitionFit: A police speed-check setup using radio echoes catches motorists going too fast.

clue.text: Follower of Charlie Brown stopped early to stalk Derek Trotter

indicators.note: to stalk is to follow behind, so this piece comes after

parts.note: Del Boy is Derek Trotter in the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses

indicators.note: stopped early means the last letter is cut off

parts.note: tan is a brown colour

explanation.surface: Charlie Brown's follower, cut short, shadows a TV wide boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie Brown' reads as the cartoon; but Charlie is a NATO alphabet code word, followed by Delta. Del Boy is the market trader of the British sitcom Only Fools and Horses.
explanation.definitionFit: In the NATO phonetic alphabet Charlie is C and the next code word stands for D.

clue.text: Electrical engineer ready to cover one lecturer on return

indicators.note: on return means the whole string is read backwards
set is placed to cover, that is to back up, the one lecturer, coming along beside them

parts.note: one is A, as in a single item
ready means set, as in ready, steady, go

explanation.surface: An engineer is prepared to stand in for a lone teacher on their return.
explanation.walkthrough: A, L and SET together are read backwards. Nikola Tesla pioneered alternating current.
explanation.definitionFit: Nikola Tesla was the Serbian-American inventor famous for alternating-current power systems.

clue.text: Women missing from second group fight

indicators.note: missing from means it is taken out

parts.note: a second group is set two

explanation.surface: No women are in the second team in a contest.
explanation.definitionFit: A brief brawl or squabble is a scrap, so this British term covers it.

clue.text: Hooter needed for how long? That's too long

indicators.note: the phrase how long is too long for the answer, so only some of its letters, sitting inside it, are kept

explanation.surface: Someone asks how long a horn or siren is needed for, then complains it's too long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooter' suggests a horn; here it is the bird, so called for its hoot.
explanation.definitionFit: This nocturnal bird hoots, so a hooter is a playful crossword name for it.

clue.text: I attach a strategy for developing extra ancient city

indicators.note: an extra is something added in, so this piece goes into the middle of the others
a plan for developing will be changed and reworked, so the letters of a strategy are rearranged

parts.note: Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: Someone ties together a growth plan with an extra mention of an old city.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue speaks as the object: 'I attach'. UR goes inside the rearranged A STRATEGY.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a short cord with metal tips used to bind papers together through punched holes, so it fastens things.

clue.text: Recurrent movement in first third of game (see 6)

indicators.note: only the opening one of the game's three parts is kept

parts.note: the game of noughts and crosses is called tic-tac-toe

explanation.surface: A repeated move in the opening period of a match, with a pointer to another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Tic-tac-toe is the American name for noughts and crosses; 6-down uses its last part.
explanation.definitionFit: An involuntary twitch that keeps happening is a recurring spasm of the muscles.

clue.text: Actress among four dancers performing legend from the East

indicators.note: among says this piece sits within the other letters
dancers performing move about, so these letters are rearranged
in an across entry, coming from the East means reading right to left, so backwards

parts.note: a legend is a traditional story or tale

explanation.surface: An actress is part of a dance quartet acting out an Eastern myth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Actress among' looks like one phrase, but the definition is just 'Actress' and 'among' is the container signal. In an across answer, 'from the East' means reading right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Frances de la Tour is a British stage and screen performer, known for Rising Damp and The History Boys.
